guides.title: What to do when
guides.html:
Dated Wednesday 18 November 2026, for the Summer 2027 cycle. Every deadline here was read off the program's own page. A program that has not posted its 2027 date is listed as not posted, never as a guess.

What changed since October. The first deadline is 4 January, not February. A run of deadlines lands between 4 and 26 January, over winter break and into the first weeks of the spring semester, and the big 1 February cluster sits right behind it. So the order of work is now:

  1. Letters and transcripts this week. Both run on somebody else's calendar.
  2. The early-January applications before you leave campus in December, while your recommenders are still easy to reach.
  3. The rest of January and the February cluster over winter break.

NIH SIP closes 26 January at noon Eastern, three weeks earlier than this site used to say. It is the best fit on the whole list for living at home in Leesburg, and NIH investigators choose their own interns, so emailing them is part of applying, not an extra.

This week: by Sunday 22 November

Already open and worth starting now: NIH SIP, Seattle Children's, MD Anderson, the Broad, Jackson Lab, Johns Hopkins Pathway, Penn SUIP, Mount Sinai, Cold Spring Harbor and both Indiana programs, among others.

  • Ask for your letters. Two recommenders, ideally your lab supervisor and one professor who knows your work. The first letters on this list are due 11 January (the Broad) and 19 January (Seattle Children's), and December is when every pre-med in the country asks. Send your CV with the request and let the rest of the packet follow. How to ask.
  • Order your official transcript. Most programs take an unofficial copy, so download that PDF as well, but some insist on an official one: every Amgen host, the Leadership Alliance (it has to arrive by 3 February, with your letters) and MSK (a signed official copy, uploaded as a PDF). Registrar offices slow down in December and close for part of winter break, so order now. If a program wants your fall grades on it, order another once those are posted.
  • Start NIH SIP. It is open now and closes 26 January at noon Eastern, with letters due 2 February at noon Eastern. It is one application that investigators all over NIH can read, and they start choosing their own interns in early January. Make the account and draft the cover letter this month.
  • Start Seattle Children's Summer Scholars. It opened 16 November and has the earliest deadline in the cycle: 4 January at 5 p.m. Pacific, which is 8 p.m. Eastern. Letters are due 19 January. Their page says applicants looking for their first formal research internship are prioritized, so if that is you, say so.
  • Bring your CV up to date. Two hours. Skeleton. Put your CITI certificates near the top: most undergraduate applicants have none.
  • Pick your list. Twelve to twenty programs is a realistic target. Set each one to Drafting in All Programs, and it moves onto My Applications, where the site tracks it for you.

Before Thanksgiving: by Wednesday 25 November

  • Give each recommender one list: every program, the date its letter is due, and how the letter gets there. The letters guide has a table to copy. Tell them how many requests to expect. Amgen alone sends a separate one for every host you choose.
  • Email NIH investigators. Pick an institute or two (NICHD for child health, NIMH for mood and anxiety, NINDS for neurology), find three to five labs whose recent papers you actually like, and email those PIs. Say that you are applying through the NIH Summer Internship Program, that you can commute from Leesburg, and when you are free. Then name them in your cover letter. Template.
  • Email the places you could commute to. Children's National, Georgetown and Inova have not posted a 2027 summer application with a deadline, so a short email to the research training or education office is the way in, and nobody else is asking yet. Janelia, in Ashburn, takes summer undergraduates through HHMI's Cech Fellows Program, which recruits from partner schools: check whether Penn State is one before you spend time on it. Why these are worth the effort is the Leesburg rule.
  • Decide the honest answer to "MD, PhD, or MD-PhD?" It changes which programs are worth the hours. Amgen and the Broad ask for an interest in a PhD or MD-PhD, Penn SUIP and the Leadership Alliance are built for students heading to a PhD, and Penn State SURIP says it is not meant for students who plan to apply to medical school. If you are aiming at medicine, spend those hours on the hospital programs instead.

Before winter break: get the early-January applications done

The first deadlines fall while you are at home and your professors are away. So the plan for December is to finish everything due by mid-January before you leave campus, or at the very least to have every letter for it requested.

  • Over Thanksgiving break, write the master personal statement. Four to six hours across a few sittings. Every application after this reuses it. Template.
  • If you want clinical research, add the biomedical CITI course. Your three CITI certificates are a real edge, since most undergraduate applicants have none, but they are the social and behavioral versions. Hospital studies mostly run under the biomedical track. The Biomedical Human Subjects Research course is a few hours online, usually free through your university, and it is what a hospital group will typically ask for before you work with patient data.
  • 1 December: Yale Child Study and UMass Chan open. Yale closes 14 January and needs two letters. UMass Chan closes 1 March.
  • CHOP CRISSP opens in December. No deadline is posted yet. Information sessions are Tuesday 8 December at 11 a.m. and Tuesday 12 January at 3 p.m. The 2027 program runs 7 June to 13 August and pays $5,000 plus free housing, with a 3.3 GPA minimum. The weekly check cannot read CHOP's page, so open it yourself every week in December.
  • Submit Seattle Children's before you leave. The deadline is 4 January, but most portals only email your recommenders once you submit your part, and Seattle's letters are due 19 January.
  • Submit St. Jude POE in December. The deadline is 1 February, but their page asks for every credential by mid-to-late December and warns that applications sent after 1 January run a high risk of not being complete in time. You need research experience outside the classroom, which your lab job should count as, and you must be able to start on 10, 17 or 24 May or 1 June.
  • Finish the 8 to 14 January applications on your list: Fred Hutch, Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program, the Broad, UPMC Children's Pittsburgh, MD Anderson and Yale Child Study. Their dates are in the next two sections.
  • Remind your recommenders before break, with the list again and the January dates at the top. Professors are hard to reach between mid-December and the new year.

Over winter break: the first deadlines

Check your email every day. Portals send confirmations, recommenders reply, and NIH investigators start getting in touch in early January.

  • 4 January, 5 p.m. Pacific (8 p.m. Eastern): Seattle Children's. The earliest deadline in the cycle.
  • 8 January, midnight Pacific (3 a.m. Eastern on 9 January): Fred Hutch SURP. Only for students entering the summer before their final year, which is you.
  • 8 January, 5 p.m. Eastern: Penn's Undergraduate Clinical Scholars Program. Clinical research, which is rare on this list. Transcripts and letters are due 15 January.
  • 10 January, 11:59 p.m. Eastern: Broad Institute BSRP. Letters by 11 January. 3.2 GPA minimum.
  • 11 January, 11:59 p.m.: UPMC Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh SRIP. 3.5 GPA minimum, sophomores and juniors.
  • Answer NIH within a day. Investigators start choosing interns in early January, and a quick reply is part of the impression you make.
  • Draft the February applications now, because January is full of its own deadlines. With the personal statement done, each one is mostly the why-this-program paragraph, twenty to thirty minutes apiece.
  • Check the NSF REU portal. Each REU site sets its own deadline, anywhere from December to March, so look once a month. Housing and travel are usually covered.

In January: the burst

  • 13 January: MD Anderson CATALYST. $7,200 for the summer. CATALYST is an umbrella over many tracks, so read its programs page and pick yours first.
  • 14 January, 5 p.m. Eastern: Yale Child Study Center. Two letters. The internship runs 7 June to 30 July.
  • 15 January: Mount Sinai SURP4US (juniors and seniors), Cold Spring Harbor URP (11:59 p.m. Pacific, $7,000), and both Indiana programs, INSPIRE and the Medical Neuroscience SURP. Letters and transcripts for Penn's Clinical Scholars Program are due the same day.
  • 16 January: the earliest Vanderbilt VSSA track. Tracks close between 16 January and 15 February, most of them on 1 February, so check the date for yours.
  • 19 January: MIT MSRP. Seattle Children's letters are due the same day.
  • 22 January: Baylor and Texas Children's SMART. $5,400 for nine weeks.
  • 25 January, 5 p.m. Eastern: Jackson Laboratory SSP.
  • 26 January, noon Eastern: NIH SIP. The letters close a week later, on 2 February at noon.
  • 31 January: Penn State PROMISE (Hershey).

Do not leave 1 February to the last week. More of this list closes that day than on any other, and it lands straight after the January burst. Have every 1 February application drafted by 20 January.

1 February to 1 March: the second wave

  • 1 February: the big cluster. Amgen Scholars (every host is its own application), St. Jude POE, Johns Hopkins Pathway SIP (11:59 p.m. Eastern, free housing, and a NeuroSIP division), Penn SUIP (11:59 p.m. Eastern, and your letters must arrive by the same deadline), Michigan SROP (11:59 p.m. Eastern), Stanford SSRP (11:59 p.m. Pacific), UCSF SRTP, Rockefeller SURF, Penn State SURIP, and MSK MBSP at 8 a.m., not end of day.
  • 2 February, 5 p.m. Eastern: NYU Langone SURP. It wants at least one full semester of bench lab research. NIH SIP letters are due at noon the same day.
  • 3 February: Leadership Alliance and Mayo Clinic SURF. The Leadership Alliance takes one application that ranks three of its 20 sites, and the whole package, letters and official transcripts included, has to arrive by the 3rd.
  • 12 February: ECU Brody SBRP.
  • 15 February: Penn State AHA-USF (Hershey, $6,000, housing at your own cost) and the last Vanderbilt tracks.
  • 1 March: UMass Chan SURP. $6,000 plus travel and housing.

Not posted yet: check these by hand

These have no 2027 deadline on their page yet. If the site shows a date for one, it is an estimate, marked est.

  • CHOP CRISSP, opening in December (above).
  • Children's National, Kennedy Krieger and Johns Hopkins JHIBS, all within reach of home.
  • Cincinnati Children's SURF, from your original list.
  • Caltech SURF. The application is a research proposal written with a prospective mentor, so that contact has to happen weeks before the deadline.
  • The rest are on the Timeline page. The weekly check flags a page when it changes, which is usually a program posting its dates. A few sites block the check, CHOP among them, and The Plan lists those for you to open by hand.

Off the list

  • SHPEP has ended. Its funder closed it, and the last cohort ran in summer 2026.
  • NYSCF requires New York City residency, so it is not open to you.
  • The Allen Institute now lists only ASPIRE, a year-long postbaccalaureate role, not a summer internship.
  • Columbia's Zuckerman Institute runs its summer programs only for Columbia and Barnard students.
  • CHLA's summer student program page is gone. The only undergraduate route there now is NIDDK's national STEP-UP program.

March to April: decisions

Decisions arrive from early March to mid-April. The Broad notifies in mid-March and Amgen by the end of March. MD Anderson wants an answer to its offers by 4 March, before many programs have decided, so know your order of preference before then.

If nothing lands: direct emails to PIs, the NIA Alzheimer's centers, and your own university's summer research funding are all still live in April. A summer in a home-campus lab with a real project is worth more than a prestigious program you did not get.

The honest summary

Four things decide this cycle, in order:

  1. Letters asked for this week. The only item gated on someone else.
  2. The early-January applications finished before winter break. Seattle Children's closes 4 January, while you are at home.
  3. Emails to PIs, NIH first. NIH investigators choose their own interns, and NIH is a commute from home.
  4. Not cramming 1 February. Draft that cluster over winter break.

Everything else is execution.

guides.title: How to get picked
guides.html:
Useful context for where to spend effort. None of this is a secret. It is just not written down anywhere an applicant naturally looks.

Who reads the application

For a large program (CHOP, St. Jude), it is usually two stages:

  1. A screen against hard criteria: eligibility, citizenship, class year, GPA floor, completeness. This stage is mechanical. Most rejections happen here and have nothing to do with how good the applicant is.
  2. Faculty review. Files get routed to labs by research area. A PI scans for: does this person want to do what we do, and can they be useful for ten weeks?

The second stage is the one worth optimizing for, and it hinges on specificity.

NIH SIP works differently. There is no central committee: individual NIH investigators read the applicant pool and choose their own interns, starting in early January. Your cover letter and your emails to PIs are the whole application there, which is why the cold email matters most at NIH.

What the screen is checking

Failing any of these wastes the whole application:

  • What you plan to do next. Amgen and the Broad ask for an interest in a PhD or MD-PhD, and Penn State SURIP says it is not meant for students who plan to apply to medical school. If you are aiming at medicine only, these screen you out as surely as a GPA floor.
  • Research experience already done. St. Jude POE requires research experience outside the classroom when you apply, and your lab job should count. NYU Langone SURP wants at least one full semester of bench lab research, which a psychology lab may not satisfy, so check with them before you spend the hours.
  • GPA floor. St. Jude wants 3.40 in science and math and 3.40 overall. UPMC Children's Pittsburgh wants 3.5, CHOP 3.3, Amgen and the Broad 3.2, and Mayo, Vanderbilt and the Leadership Alliance 3.0. These are hard filters.
  • Class year. Fred Hutch takes only students entering the summer before their final year, which is you. Many programs exclude students who graduate before or during the summer, and Seattle Children's excludes anyone graduating before or during the program.
  • Availability for the full term. St. Jude requires one of four specific start dates (10, 17 or 24 May, or 1 June) and eleven weeks from undergraduates. The Broad requires all nine weeks. If you have a conflict, address it before applying, not after.
  • Completeness. Letters that arrive after the deadline sink otherwise strong applications. St. Jude's deadline covers every credential, and Penn SUIP's letters must arrive by the application deadline itself.
  • Citizenship and residency. NSF REUs want a US citizen, US national or permanent resident, and NIH SIP, Amgen and many others ask for much the same. As a US citizen you clear all of these. Residency is the exception: NYSCF takes only New York City residents, which is why it is off your list.

The site's filters exist mostly to stop you spending four hours on a program you are not eligible for. Fill in My eligibility and the site flags every program that conflicts, with the reason.

What the faculty review is weighing

Roughly in order:

  1. Fit with a specific lab. The single biggest factor, and the one most within your control. An application that names a PI, references their work, and says why, lands in a different pile. If you have emailed that PI and they said yes, it is a different pile again.
  2. Evidence of follow-through. Ten weeks is short. They are looking for signs someone will not need babysitting: a project you ran, a protocol you handled, a semester of consistent lab hours, a job that required showing up.
  3. A real reason for the area. Not passion, a question. "I want to understand why seizure burden predicts developmental outcome" tells a reader where to route the file.
  4. Letters. Mostly used as corroboration. A detailed letter from someone who supervised you beats a glowing one from someone who taught you in a lecture.
  5. Grades and coursework. Matter at the screen, matter less here, as long as the relevant courses are there.

What does not move the needle

  • Enthusiasm as such. Everyone is enthusiastic.
  • Volume of extracurriculars unrelated to research or clinical work.
  • Prestige-signaling about the program in the essay. They know it is good.
  • A longer personal statement. Over-length is a mild negative.

The four asymmetries worth exploiting

One application, many labs. NIH SIP, the Leadership Alliance and Vanderbilt's VSSA each put a single application in front of many labs or institutions. Investigators all over NIH can read your SIP application, the Leadership Alliance application ranks three of its 20 sites, and VSSA runs many tracks through one portal. The marginal cost of the second, third and fifth lab is small. These should be done first and done well.

Amgen Scholars is the near miss. There is no single Amgen application: each of the 14 US hosts runs its own, with its own portal and its own letter request to your recommenders. The essays are reusable and the paperwork is not, so count each extra host as half an application rather than a free one, and tell your recommenders how many there will be.

Cold emails. Fifteen minutes, and the only thing that converts an anonymous file into a named candidate. Most applicants never send one. At NIH they are part of the application. Template.

Less-famous places with real research. Arkansas Children's, Stowers, Van Andel, UAB, Einstein, Nemours and Benaroya do genuine work and receive a fraction of the applications that CHOP and St. Jude get. A summer with a real project and a mentor who had time beats a rejection from a famous program. Build the list with a few of these in it deliberately.

Living at home. A program you can commute to is worth more than its stipend says, because none of it goes on rent. NIH, Janelia, Inova, Children's National and Georgetown are all within reach of Leesburg, and so, at a stretch, are Hopkins and Kennedy Krieger in Baltimore. See the Leesburg rule.

On the thin-experience problem

If your research experience is light, that is normal going into your senior-year summer, and several programs are built for it. Seattle Children's says on its own page that prior formal research experience is not required and that applicants seeking their first formal research internship are prioritized. NSF REUs are designed as entry points.

Two on this list go the other way, and it is a mechanical screen rather than a judgment call. St. Jude POE requires research experience outside the classroom at the time you apply. NYU Langone SURP wants at least one full semester of bench lab research. Check those two before you spend the hours.

What helps: a serious course project described as research, specific technical skills you can actually perform, and a letter from someone who has watched you work. What does not help: apologizing for it in the personal statement.

A realistic expectation

These programs run acceptance rates in the low single digits to low teens. Strong applicants get rejected from most places they apply. The right response is volume on the reusable applications plus a handful of genuinely attainable targets, not six perfect applications to six famous programs.

Twelve to twenty applications is a reasonable target for this cycle, and the structure in this repo is built to make that a realistic amount of work rather than an impossible one.

guides.title: Reading a program page
guides.html:
Program pages bury the things that decide whether an application is worth starting. This is the order to look for them.

The five disqualifiers. Check these first

Before reading a single word about the research, find:

  1. Citizenship requirement. "US citizen or permanent resident" appears on most federally funded programs. As a US citizen you clear this one, so look for residency rules instead: NYSCF takes only New York City residents, which is why it is no longer on the site.
  2. Class year. Look for "rising senior", "must have completed sophomore year", "may not graduate before/during the program". Fred Hutch takes only students entering the summer before their final year, which is you. Seattle Children's turns away anyone graduating before or during the program.
  3. GPA minimum. Often in a FAQ rather than the main page.
  4. Dates. Fixed start dates (St. Jude has four and only four), and whether the full term is mandatory.
  5. Deadline, and what it covers. Specifically: are letters due on the same date, or later? Penn SUIP's letters must arrive by the application deadline itself. The Broad gives letters one extra day, and Seattle Children's gives them fifteen. St. Jude's deadline covers every credential.

If any of these rule you out, stop. That is a win, four hours saved.

Then find the mentor list

The most valuable page on any program site, and often two clicks deep: "Faculty", "Mentors", "Research areas", "Labs", or a PDF of last year's projects.

This is where the why-this-program paragraph and the cold emails come from. A program with no published mentor list is one where naming a mentor matters less, and a program with a long list is one where naming a mentor matters a great deal.

Then the practicalities

  • Stipend, and whether housing is separate. The two numbers only mean something together. A $7,500 stipend with room, board and travel included (Jackson Lab at Bar Harbor) is worth far more than $5,000 with no housing in Boston.
  • Housing: provided, subsidized, or your problem. "Not provided" is only bad news if you have to pay rent, which is what the Leesburg rule below is about.
  • Travel: Jackson Lab and several others reimburse it; most do not.
  • Length: usually ten weeks, sometimes eight or nine (St. Jude wants eleven from undergraduates), and whether it collides with the end of your spring semester.

The dataset already has all of this, but verify it on the page before applying. The stipend figures in particular are the fields most likely to be stale.

The Leesburg rule

A program you can commute to from home is worth a smaller stipend, because housing is free at home. With no rent to pay, a stipend with no housing is the whole stipend. The same offer in Seattle, Boston or New York loses most of it to rent.

Within reach of Leesburg, roughly, without traffic:

  • Janelia in Ashburn, about 15 minutes. Its summer undergraduates come through HHMI's Cech Fellows Program, which recruits from partner schools, so check whether Penn State is one.
  • Inova in Fairfax, about 35 minutes.
  • NIH in Bethesda, about 45 minutes. NIH SIP provides no housing, which does not matter when you are driving in from home.
  • Children's National and Georgetown in Washington, about an hour.
  • Johns Hopkins and Kennedy Krieger in Baltimore, about 70 minutes. A long commute, but a real one, and Hopkins Pathway houses its interns for free anyway.

So when you compare offers, compare what you keep. A smaller stipend near home can beat a bigger one in a city where you pay rent.

Signs the page is from a previous cycle

Still common, because plenty of 2027 pages have not been updated yet:

  • Dates in 2025 or 2026 with no mention of 2027
  • "Applications are closed", "check back in the fall", "will open in November"
  • A deadline that has already passed

None of these mean the program is gone. They mean the new cycle is not posted. Note the date and let the weekly check catch the update. You do not have to run anything: it runs every Monday on its own, and what it found sits at the top of The Plan. A page that changes, and especially one that starts mentioning 2027, is usually a program posting its new dates.

One thing it cannot do. A few sites refuse an automated reader, so the check never sees them at all. CHOP CRISSP, which opens in December, is one of them. The Plan lists every one under the note that says those sites block the weekly check. Open those pages yourself every couple of weeks, because nothing is going to tell you when they post.

When the page says almost nothing

Some real programs have one thin paragraph and an email address. That is not a bad sign. It often means placements are arranged directly rather than through a portal, which is good news for anyone willing to write an email.

In that case skip the application entirely and go straight to a cold email to the listed contact or to a relevant PI. The NIA Alzheimer's centers, UCSF pediatrics and the UC Davis MIND Institute all work this way, and so do two of the places you could commute to: Georgetown and Inova post a page about research and training rather than a summer application with a deadline.

guides.title: Personal statement
guides.html:
Write this once, properly. Then every application becomes: paste the master, swap the program-specific paragraph, adjust length. That is the difference between applying to six programs and applying to twenty.

Target length: 600-800 words. Most programs ask for 500-1000, and a tight 650 reads better than a padded 950.

The shape

Paragraph 1, the specific thing that got you here (100-150 words)

Not "I have always loved science." One concrete moment, experience or question, and what it made you want to find out. If there is a personal reason behind the pediatric interest, this is where it goes, stated plainly, once, without reaching for drama.

Weak: "Ever since I was young, I have been fascinated by the human brain."

Better: "[CONCRETE MOMENT]. What stuck with me was not [the obvious part] but [the specific thing you noticed]. I wanted to know [the actual question]."

Paragraph 2, what you have actually done (150-200 words)

Research experience, coursework that genuinely matters, lab skills, clinical or volunteer work. For each thing: what the question was, what you did, and what you learned about doing research, not just what the project was about.

Committees read for evidence that someone can be trusted with ten weeks of a mentor's time. Signals that help: you ran something independently, you handled a protocol, you dealt with a result that did not work.

"In [COURSE/LAB], I [SPECIFIC TASK, the assay, the dataset, the protocol]. [WHAT WENT WRONG OR SURPRISED YOU]. That taught me [SOMETHING REAL ABOUT RESEARCH, not a platitude]."

If you have little or no formal research experience: say so without apology and lean on transferable evidence, a hard course with a project component, a data analysis you did, a job that required precision and follow-through. Seattle Children's says outright that prior formal research experience is not required, and it prioritizes applicants seeking their first formal research internship.

Paragraph 3, what you want to work on (120-180 words)

The research area, and why. Be specific enough that a reader could guess which labs to route the application to. "Pediatric neurology, particularly how seizure burden affects development" is useful. "Biomedical research" is not.

Naming a method or model system helps: EEG, mouse models, patient-registry data, imaging, single-cell work.

Paragraph 4, why this program, specifically (100-150 words)

The one paragraph that changes every time. See the why-this-program guide. Never send an application where this paragraph could have been addressed to any other institution.

Paragraph 5, where this goes (80-120 words)

MD, PhD, MD-PhD, or honestly undecided between them, all fine. What is not fine is vagueness that reads as not having thought about it. If undecided, say what the summer would help you decide.

Note: Amgen Scholars, the Broad, Penn SUIP, the Leadership Alliance, MIT MSRP and WashU's BioMedRAP are PhD-pipeline programs, and Penn State SURIP says it is not meant for students who plan to apply to medical school. If you are aiming MD-only, those are a weaker fit than the hospital-based programs, and the statement should not pretend otherwise.

Before sending, check

  • Could this paragraph have been written by any other applicant? Rewrite it.
  • Does the program name appear, spelled correctly, in paragraph 4?
  • Is there at least one specific paper, lab or faculty member named?
  • Any sentence beginning "I am passionate about"? Delete it.
  • Read aloud, anywhere you stumble, a reader will too.
  • Within the word limit. Over-length gets cut or counted against.
  • Someone else proofread it. Not spellcheck, a person.

Three openings that work

  1. The question. Open with the thing you genuinely want to know, then how you came to care about it.
  2. The moment. A specific scene, in a lab, a clinic, a classroom, and the question it raised. Earns its place only if it leads somewhere.
  3. The problem. Something unresolved in the field, and where you want to stand in relation to it. Strongest option if you have read real literature; risky if you have not.

Avoid: quotations from famous scientists, dictionary definitions, "webster's defines", and childhood-illness framing unless it is genuinely yours to tell.

guides.title: CV skeleton
guides.html:
One page. Two only if there is genuinely a second page of content, which at this stage there usually is not.

A research CV is not a job resume. Drop the objective statement, drop "Microsoft Office", and lead with education and research.

Wherever the skeleton says [TAB], the part after it sits flush against the right margin. How to do that in Google Docs or Word, without spaces, is the first rule below the skeleton.

[FULL NAME]
[email] · [phone] · [city, state] · [LinkedIn or ORCID, if either exists]


EDUCATION

[University] [TAB] [City, State]
Bachelor of Science in [Major], expected [Month Year] [TAB] GPA: [X.XX / 4.00]
Minor in [X]
Relevant coursework: [4-6 courses that matter, biochem, neuroscience,
statistics, organic chemistry, research methods. Not intro bio.]
[Honors, dean's list, scholarships]


RESEARCH EXPERIENCE

[Lab or Project Name], [Institution] [TAB] [Month Year] to present
Supervisor: [Dr. Name]
· [What the lab studies, in one line of plain English.]
· [What YOU did, the technique, the assay, the dataset, the protocol.
  Start with a verb. "Performed," "Analyzed," "Maintained," "Coded."]
· [A result, output or responsibility: a poster, a presentation, a dataset
  you owned, a protocol you ran unsupervised.]

[Course-based research, independent project, or honors thesis also goes here.
A serious semester project counts as research experience. Say what the question
was and what you did.]


CERTIFICATIONS

[CITI Program: Human Subjects Research, and which track] [TAB] [Month Year]
[CITI Program: Good Clinical Practice] [TAB] [Month Year]
[A clinical certification, such as EMT] [TAB] [Month Year]


CLINICAL & VOLUNTEER EXPERIENCE

[Role], [Organization] [TAB] [Month Year] to [Month Year]
· [What you did and roughly how many hours.]
· [Anything involving responsibility, patients, or data.]


TECHNICAL SKILLS

Laboratory: [PCR, cell culture, Western blot, immunohistochemistry, microscopy;
only things you could do unsupervised tomorrow]
Data: [R, Python, SPSS, Excel, REDCap, GraphPad Prism]
Other: [Spanish (conversational), IRB protocol experience]


PRESENTATIONS & PUBLICATIONS
[Only if real. Poster at a campus symposium counts and should be listed.]

[Last, F.] et al. "[Title]." [Venue], [Year]. [Poster / oral presentation]


AWARDS & HONORS

[Award], [Granting body] [TAB] [Year]

Rules that matter

  • Do not fake the right-hand column with spaces. The skeleton marks it with [TAB] because spaces do not survive the trip into a word processor: in Google Docs or Word every run of spaces lands somewhere different and the right edge comes out ragged. Use a right-aligned tab stop. In Google Docs, click the ruler at the right margin and add a right tab stop there. In Word, open the Paragraph settings, choose Tabs, and set a right-aligned tab at the right margin. Then press Tab once wherever the skeleton says [TAB]. A two-column table with the borders turned off works too. Both survive editing and the PDF export.
  • Use the bullet button for the · lines instead of typing the dots, so a bullet that wraps onto a second line stays indented.
  • Reverse chronological within every section.
  • No pronouns. "Performed immunostaining," not "I performed immunostaining."
  • Verbs first. Not "Was responsible for maintaining cell cultures" but "Maintained cell cultures."
  • Be specific about skills. "Proficient in laboratory techniques" says nothing. "Mouse colony management, genotyping by PCR" says a lot.
  • Quantify where it is honest. "Enrolled 40 patients," "analyzed 12 months of registry data."
  • Certifications near the top. CITI human subjects and Good Clinical Practice training is something most undergraduate applicants do not have, so do not bury it under skills.
  • One page, 10-11pt, generous margins. A cramped two-pager reads worse than a clean one-pager.
  • Export to PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-CV.pdf. Never send a .docx.

If the research section is thin

Common, and not disqualifying. Seattle Children's says prior formal research experience is not required and prioritizes applicants seeking their first formal research internship, and plenty of others take students with no bench experience at all.

What to do: promote a serious course project into the research section with its real question and method. List coursework that signals readiness (statistics, biochem, a lab-heavy course). Put technical skills higher so they are seen early. Do not pad with high-school material.

guides.title: Asking for letters
guides.html:
Most programs on this list want two letters. The same two letters go everywhere, so this is a one-time cost, but only if you ask early and make it easy.

Ask as soon as you read this. The first letters on this list are due in January, not February: the Broad's on 11 January, Seattle Children's on 19 January, and NIH's on 2 February. Penn SUIP wants its letters by the application deadline itself, 1 February. Faculty write letters in batches, and December is when every pre-med in the country is asking. A request in November gives them weeks. One sent in January does not.

Who to ask

In order of usefulness:

  1. A research mentor: anyone who has seen you work in a lab, even briefly. Nothing else is as persuasive.
  2. A professor from a small, hard course where you spoke up and did well. A seminar or lab course beats a 400-person lecture every time.
  3. Someone you work for as a learning or teaching assistant. They have watched you show up and follow through, which is most of what a letter is for.
  4. A clinical or volunteer supervisor, if the program is clinically oriented.

Avoid: a famous professor who cannot pick you out of a crowd. A detailed letter from a postdoc beats a vague one from a department chair.

The email

Subject: Letter of recommendation request, summer research programs (first letter due [EARLIEST LETTER DATE])

Dear Professor [NAME],

I am applying to summer 2027 undergraduate research programs in [AREA], and I am hoping you would be willing to write me a letter of recommendation.

I took [COURSE] with you in [TERM] and [SPECIFIC THING, the project you did, something you contributed, the grade if it is good]. [IF A RESEARCH MENTOR: what you worked on and what you handled independently.]

I am applying to about [NUMBER] programs. The first letter is due [EARLIEST LETTER DATE] and the last on [LATEST LETTER DATE]. Most programs collect letters through an online form that emails you a link once I submit my part, so you would get one email per program. I have attached the full list, with each date and how each letter is submitted, and I will send a reminder before every deadline so you do not have to track any of it.

I have also attached my CV, my draft personal statement, and a short note on what I have been doing since your course.

Would you be willing? If you do not feel you could write a strong letter, I would completely understand. I would rather know now.

Thank you for considering it.

[NAME]

Fill both dates from your own list. If the Broad is on it, the first letter is due 11 January.

That last paragraph of the email matters. It gives a lukewarm writer a graceful exit, which is far better than a tepid letter you never see.

If your personal statement is not drafted yet, send the request anyway with the CV and say the statement will follow within two weeks. Waiting for a perfect packet costs more than it gains.

The one list to send each recommender

One page, one row per program, in date order. It is the most useful thing you can give a recommender, because it turns twenty separate emails into one plan. Copy this table and fill in your own programs. The date comes from the program's page on the site, and how the letter is submitted comes from the program's own page.

ProgramLetter dueHow the letter is submitted
Broad Institute BSRP11 January, 11:59 p.m. Eastern[a link the portal emails you, an upload, or an email address]
Seattle Children's Summer Scholars19 January, 5 p.m. Pacific[how]
NIH Summer Internship Program2 February, noon Eastern[how]
Penn SUIP1 February, 11:59 p.m. Eastern, same as the application[how]
[Program][Date, time and time zone][how]

The four filled rows are real dates. Keep the ones you are applying to and add the rest.

Three things make the list work:

  • Put a time zone on every date. Seattle's is Pacific, NIH's is Eastern, and a professor reading "5 p.m." will assume their own.
  • Give each Amgen host its own row. Each host is a separate application and sends its own request, so five hosts means five emails.
  • Flag the ones where letters are due with the application, like Penn SUIP, so they get done first.

The packet to attach

Everything that makes writing easier makes the letter better:

  1. CV: current.
  2. Personal statement: the draft is fine. It tells them the story to corroborate.
  3. The one list above: only your programs, with letter dates and how each is submitted. Not the whole spreadsheet from the site.
  4. A reminder of who you are: a short paragraph: the course, the term, what you did well, anything memorable. Professors teach hundreds of students a year and this is a kindness, not an imposition.
  5. What to emphasize: if a program wants independence, say so.

Managing it afterwards

  • Add each recommender under Who is writing your letters on My Applications, and update their status as they reply. Note anything program-specific in that program's notes.
  • Most portals email the recommender a link only after you submit your part. Submit early so they have runway. St. Jude explicitly says to submit without waiting for letters.
  • Send a reminder ten days before each deadline if the portal still shows the letter as outstanding. For anything due in January, send it before winter break instead: professors are hard to reach over the holidays.
  • Thank them afterwards, and tell them the outcome either way. They are going to be asked again for medical school.

The honest timing note

A letter requested on 2 January for an 11 January deadline will be written in a hurry and will read like it. The same professor asked in November writes a better letter for the same student. The quality difference is entirely in the lead time.

guides.title: Emailing a lab
guides.html:
The highest-return thing in this whole repo, and almost nobody does it.

Many summer programs ask applicants to name preferred mentors, and a fair number of placements come down to a faculty member saying "I would take this student." At NIH it is the whole process. The Summer Internship Program has no central selection: individual investigators choose their own interns, starting in early January, so an email to an NIH lab is part of applying. Several entries on this list, the Boston Children's epilepsy lab, the UC Davis MIND Institute, the NIA Alzheimer's centers, UCSF pediatrics, and the hospitals near home that post no summer application, such as Georgetown and Inova, are effectively only reachable this way.

A good cold email takes fifteen minutes. Send three or four per program you seriously want, and three to five to NIH labs before winter break.

The rules

  1. Short. Under 200 words. They are reading it on a phone between meetings.
  2. Specific. Name one of their papers and say something true about it. Generic praise is worse than none.
  3. Ask for one thing. Not "please mentor me for the summer", just whether they are taking a summer student.
  4. Answer "who pays" and "when" before they ask. Those are the first two questions in a PI's head. Name the program you are applying through and say that it pays your stipend, then give the dates you are free. An email that answers both reads as a student who can be slotted into a plan. One that leaves them open reads as a request for money and a scheduling problem.
  5. Attach the CV. One PDF, named Lastname-Firstname-CV.pdf.
  6. Subject line that survives a crowded inbox.
  7. No follow-up for ten days. Then exactly one, and never a third.

Template

Subject: Summer 2027 [PROGRAM] applicant interested in [THEIR TOPIC]

Dear Dr. [LAST NAME],

I am a [YEAR] at [SCHOOL] studying [MAJOR], and I am applying to [PROGRAM NAME] for summer 2027. I am writing because I would like to work in your lab.

I read your [YEAR] paper on [SPECIFIC TOPIC, the actual finding, not the title]. [ONE SENTENCE THAT SHOWS YOU READ IT: something that surprised you, a question it raised, how it connects to what you want to understand.]

My background: [ONE SENTENCE, relevant coursework, lab experience, technique]. [IF APPLICABLE: a sentence on what you can already do that is useful: participant sessions, data coding, R or Python, data entry on a clinical study. Name your CITI human subjects and Good Clinical Practice training here. It is the gate on work with patients or study participants, and most undergraduates have not done it.]

[PROGRAM NAME] pays its interns a stipend, so I would not need funding from the lab. I am free from [START DATE] to [END DATE], full time. [IF YOU COULD COMMUTE: I live in Leesburg, so I do not need housing.]

Are you taking a summer student in 2027? If the program application should name a preferred mentor, I would like to name you, but only if that would be welcome.

My CV is attached. Thank you for your time.

[FULL NAME] [SCHOOL], Class of [YEAR] [EMAIL] · [PHONE]

The stipend sentence is the one most applicants leave out, and it changes how the whole email reads. Check the program page first: nearly every program on this list pays a stipend, but write only what is true. If there is no program behind the email, as with a hospital that posts no summer application, leave that sentence out and ask instead whether the lab has a summer program you could apply through.

For NIH, name the NIH Summer Internship Program, say whether you have already submitted the application, and name the same PIs in your cover letter.

Finding the right PI

  1. Open the program page, find the faculty or mentor list.
  2. No list? Search the department site for the research area. For NIH, search the Intramural Research Program by topic and look at the institute: NICHD for child health, NIMH for mood and anxiety, NINDS for neurology.
  3. Open two or three recent papers from each candidate on PubMed. If the abstracts bore you, you have saved yourself a summer.
  4. Check they are actually active. A lab whose last paper was 2019 may be winding down.
  5. Get the email from the faculty page, not from a paper's corresponding-author line, which is often stale.

What a reply looks like

  • "Yes, name me": excellent. Put it in the application immediately and say so explicitly: "Dr. X has agreed to host me." That line is worth a lot. At NIH, a yes means the PI will look for your application, so make sure it is submitted.
  • "I am not taking students but talk to Dr. Y": a warm introduction. Use it.
  • "Apply through the central program": neutral, but you are now a name they have seen rather than one of 400 files.
  • Silence: the normal outcome. Not personal. Send more.

Worth knowing

Expect most emails to go unanswered. Ten emails producing one "yes" is a good rate, and that one yes can decide the summer. The failure mode is not sending them at all.

guides.title: Why this program
guides.html:
The only part of the application that cannot be reused, which is exactly why it carries so much weight. A committee can tell in one sentence whether an applicant looked at their page for ninety seconds or for twenty minutes.

Budget 20-30 minutes per program. That is the whole cost.

What goes in it

Three things, in roughly 100-150 words:

  1. Something only true of this program. A named faculty member, a center, a specific resource, the structure of the summer.
  2. Why that matches what you want to do. The connection stated explicitly: do not make the reader infer it.
  3. What you would bring. One line, concrete.

The research, in four steps

  1. Open the program page. Find the faculty or mentor list. This is the part worth the time.
  2. Pick two or three names whose work genuinely interests you.
  3. Look up one recent paper from each on PubMed. Read the abstract properly and skim the figures.
  4. Write the paragraph naming one or two of them and what specifically draws you.

A worked example

Vague, could be sent anywhere:

I am excited to apply to your program because of its strong reputation in pediatric research and the excellent mentorship it provides. I believe this program would help me grow as a researcher and prepare me for medical school.

Specific, could only be sent to this program:

I am applying to CRISSP because of the breadth of pediatric neurology work at CHOP, and Dr. [NAME]'s group in particular. Their 2025 paper on [TOPIC] found [SPECIFIC FINDING], which surprised me because [HONEST REACTION]. I have been trying to understand [RELATED QUESTION] since [YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE], and CHOP has the patient volume to ask it properly. I would come in able to [CONCRETE SKILL], and I am most interested in the [SPECIFIC METHOD] side of the work.

The second version is not better writing. It is better research.

Per-program angles for the top picks

Pulled from the dataset. Use these as the starting point:

ProgramThe thing to name
NIH SIPThere is no central committee: NIH investigators read the applicant pool and choose their own interns, so your cover letter is the paragraph that matters. Name the institute (NICHD for child health, NIMH for mood and anxiety, NINDS for neurology), two or three specific intramural labs, and the PIs you have emailed.
Amgen ScholarsEach host is a separate application, so the paragraph must be about that campus, not about Amgen.
Jackson LaboratoryThe independent-project structure and the written report. They care that applicants want to own a project.
Fred Hutch SURPRising-seniors-only. Say explicitly that this is your last summer before applying onward, and what you want to settle.
Leadership AllianceOne application ranks three of its 20 sites, so name all three and say why each. The end-of-summer national symposium is a real draw, so mention presenting. It is built for students heading to a PhD.
St. Jude POEPediatric oncology specifically. They want people who want this, not generic biomedical research. Pitch the laboratory side: St. Jude reserves clinical research placements for students already in medical school, so a paragraph asking for clinical work asks for the one thing they cannot offer you. Check the 3.40 GPA floor and the four fixed start dates before you spend the twenty minutes.
Vanderbilt VSSAName the sub-track (neuroscience, cancer biology, immunology) rather than the umbrella.
Boston Children's epilepsy labA single lab: the paragraph is effectively a cold email. Name Dr. Loddenkemper's work directly.
CHOP CRISSPEnormous institution; naming a division and a faculty member is what separates applications.
Seattle Children'sTheir page says applicants seeking their first formal research internship are prioritized. If this would be your first, that is an argument for you here. Make it.
Yale Child Study CenterChild development and child mental health. Name the lab and the age group or condition it studies, and connect it to the mood and anxiety work you already do.

Check before sending

  • Program name spelled correctly, and it is the right program
  • At least one faculty member or center named
  • At least one specific paper, finding, or resource referenced
  • No sentence that would survive a find-and-replace of the institution name
  • The "what I bring" line is concrete, not a feeling

guides.title: How to use all this
guides.html:
Everything in here is a starting point, not a finished document. The parts in [SQUARE BRACKETS] are the parts only you can fill in, and they are the only parts a reader actually cares about.

The one idea worth internalizing

Almost every applicant writes some version of "I have always been passionate about helping children and I am eager to learn." Selection committees read hundreds of those. They are not evidence of anything.

What gets someone selected is specificity: a particular question you find interesting, a particular reason this lab can answer it, and some evidence you can be useful in a lab for ten weeks. One concrete sentence about a paper you read beats three paragraphs of enthusiasm.

What to build, in order

Letters come first, because they are the only thing here that runs on somebody else's calendar, and the first ones are due in January.

#ThingTimeReuse
1Recommendation requests30 min per recommenderSame letter goes everywhere
2Official transcript15 min to order, days to arriveEvery program that insists on an official copy
3CV2 hours onceEvery application
4Master personal statement4-6 hours once~80% reusable
5Cold emails to PIs15 min eachHighest leverage, lowest effort
6Per-program paragraph20-30 min eachNever reusable. This is the point

Guides worth reading before writing:

  • The timeline: what to do between now and February
  • How to actually get picked: what these committees weigh
  • Reading a program page: finding the real requirements fast, and the Leesburg rule

The site around these documents

These guides sit inside a site, and a few parts of it are easy to miss:

  • The Plan is the page for a normal day: what is open, what is due next, what the weekly check found on Monday, and which sites it cannot read.
  • All Programs has every program, with filters for research area, deadline month, housing, stipend and citizenship. Open a program for its eligibility, stipend, housing and requirements checklist.
  • My eligibility takes your year, GPA and citizenship and flags every program that conflicts with them, with the reason.
  • My Applications tracks each application, and its Who is writing your letters panel keeps track of your recommenders.
  • Back it up. Your progress is saved in this browser only. Press Backup at the top of the page once a week and keep the file somewhere safe. Restore brings it back on a new laptop or after you clear your browser.
  • Add to calendar downloads every opening date and deadline as a calendar file. Export spreadsheet downloads the whole list.
  • Your Claude kit has the files to attach to a Claude chat so it can help you fill in forms and draft emails.

The highest-leverage thing on this whole list

Cold-emailing PIs. Most programs let applicants name a preferred mentor, and many placements are effectively decided by whether a specific faculty member said "I would take this student." At NIH it is the whole process, because investigators choose their own interns. A short, specific email to three or four PIs per program moves the odds more than another round of polishing the personal statement. Template here.
